::: {.callout-warning}
The extension interface is under active development and may change without warning. Do not rely on stability of manifest fields, module protocol, or resolution behavior until this warning is removed.
:::

# What is an extension?

An extension is a directory with an `extension.toml` manifest. It is the single unit of distribution and customization in *Calepin*. An extension can bundle any combination of:

- A **target** definition (writer, modules, post-processing)
- **Templates** (template overrides for elements and pages)
- **Modules** (structural transforms, auto-numbering, external code)
- **Assets** (CSS, JS, fonts, images, static files)
- **Vars** (default variables available in templates, overridable by the user)

An extension can be as small as a manifest plus one CSS file, or as large as a full presentation framework with templates, modules, and scripts.

Built-in targets (`html`, `latex`, `typst`, `markdown`, `slides`, `website`, `book`) are also extensions internally. The same architecture applies everywhere.


# Key concepts

- **Extension** -- A directory with an `extension.toml` manifest. The unit of distribution.
- **Target** -- An output profile: which writer to use, which modules to run, which file extension to produce. Defined in the `[target]` section of the manifest.
- **Writer** -- One of the four rendering engines: `html`, `latex`, `typst`, `markdown`. Every target has exactly one writer. Writers are not user-extensible.
- **Template** -- A Jinja template that renders a specific element or page component (e.g., `figure.html`, `page.tex`). Resolved by name through a layered chain. Adding a template is enough to create a custom div style.
- **Module** -- A declared transform in the manifest. Only needed when templates alone are insufficient: structural transforms, match rules beyond class names, auto-numbering, or external code.
- **Asset** -- A CSS, JS, or static file declared in `[assets]`. CSS and JS are injected into the page template; static files are copied to the output directory.
- **Vars** -- Key-value pairs declared in `[vars]`. Namespaced by extension name in templates: `{{ vars.tufte.sidenote_style }}`. Users override them in front matter under `[vars.extension_name]`.


# Directory layout

```
my-extension/
  extension.toml        # Manifest (required)
  templates/            # Template overrides
    html/
      page.html
      figure.html
    common/
      note.jinja
  assets/               # CSS, JS, images, fonts
    tufte.css
    tufte.js
  scripts/              # External module executables (scripts, WASM)
    postprocess.sh
    transform.wasm
```

All subdirectories are optional. Module declarations live in `extension.toml` itself. There are no separate `module.toml` files. Module templates are resolved from `templates/` like any other template (matched by class name). External executables live in `scripts/`.


# The manifest

The manifest is the complete index of everything the extension provides. Nothing is discovered by directory scanning.

## Metadata and inheritance

```toml
name = "tufte"
description = "Tufte-style HTML with sidenotes and margin notes"
version = "1.0.0"
author = "Jane Doe"
license = "MIT"

# Single-chain inheritance: exactly one parent.
inherits = "html"
```

The `inherits` field names exactly one parent: a built-in target or another installed extension. Resolution is recursive with cycle detection. Fields in the child override fields in the parent. `Vec` fields (modules, post, fig_formats) use all-or-nothing: if the child specifies the field, it replaces the parent's list entirely; if omitted, the parent's list is inherited.

## Target definition

```toml
[target]
writer = "html"                     # inherited if omitted
extension = "html"                  # output file extension; inherited if omitted
template = "page"                   # page template name; inherited if omitted
fig_extension = "svg"               # default figure extension; inherited if omitted
preview = "serve"                   # "serve", "open", or "none"; inherited if omitted
standalone = true                   # self-contained file (inline CSS/JS, base64 images)
crossref = "html"                   # "html", "latex", or "plain"; inherited if omitted
toc_headings = true                 # pass headings to page template for TOC

# Modules: full ordered list. Replaces parent's module list entirely.
# Omit to inherit parent's modules unchanged.
modules = ["highlight", "append_footnotes", "sidenotes", "embed_images"]

# Post-processing commands. Run in order after rendering.
# {input} = rendered file, {output} = final output path.
post = ["pagefind --site {output}"]

# Preferred figure formats, in priority order.
fig_formats = ["svg", "png", "jpg"]
```

## Variables

```toml
# Namespaced under the extension name in templates.
# Available as {{ vars.tufte.sidenote_style }}.
# Users override in front matter: [vars.tufte] sidenote_style = "popup"
[vars]
sidenote_style = "margin"
cdn = "https://cdn.example.com/tufte"
```

## Assets

```toml
# Paths are relative to the extension directory.
# CSS files are injected into the page template via {{ css }}.
# JS files are injected via {{ js }}.
# Static files are copied to assets/ in the output directory.
[assets]
css = ["tufte.css"]
js = ["tufte.js"]
static = ["fonts/"]
```

## Modules {#modules}

Most extensions do not need `[[modules]]` entries at all. If you just want a custom div style, add a template to `templates/{writer}/` and use `::: {.my-class}`. The template is resolved by class name automatically.

Declare a `[[modules]]` entry only when you need capabilities beyond what a template provides:

- Match by attribute, id prefix, or writer (not just class)
- Structural transforms (rewrite children before rendering)
- Auto-numbering (`number = true`)
- External code (`run = "scripts/foo.sh"` or `run = "scripts/foo.wasm"`)

```toml
# Structural transform module
[[modules]]
name = "sidenotes"
description = "Convert footnotes to margin sidenotes"
kind = "element_children"
contexts = ["div"]

[modules.match]
classes = ["sidenote", "margin-note"]
# attrs = ["sidenote-ref"]          # attribute names (OR'd with classes)
# id_prefix = "sn-"                 # ID prefix trigger
# writers = ["html"]                # restrict to writers (omit = all)
# number = true                     # auto-number matching divs

# External module (script or WASM)
# [[modules]]
# name = "rewrite-links"
# description = "Rewrite external links to open in new tab"
# kind = "document"
# run = "scripts/rewrite-links.sh"  # .wasm for WASM runtime

# Project module (cross-page coordination)
# [[modules]]
# name = "site_wrap"
# description = "Wrap pages in site template with navigation"
# kind = "project"
```


# Module kinds

| `kind` | When it runs | What it receives | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| `span` | During render, per span | One span | Renders matching bracketed spans |
| `element_children` | During render, per div | One div's children | Rewrites div children (structural transforms) |
| `element` | Pre-render | One element | Mutates individual elements before rendering |
| `document` | Post-assembly, per page | One page's document string | Transforms a single page |
| `project` | After all pages rendered | All rendered pages + config | Cross-page coordination (navigation, cross-refs, site wrapping) |

The first four kinds operate on a single page. The `project` kind operates on the full set of rendered pages at once. This is how multi-document features (websites, books) work without needing a separate pipeline.

For single documents, the pipeline renders one page and no `project` modules run. For multi-document projects (when `[[contents]]` is present in config), pages are discovered and rendered in parallel, then `project` modules coordinate across them.


# Templates vs. modules

**Templates alone** handle most customization. Add `templates/html/note.html` to your extension and `::: {.note}` renders using that template. No module declaration needed. The template receives standard variables (content, classes, attrs, id, etc.) and is overridable at every level of the resolution chain.

**Modules** add behavior that templates cannot express: structural transforms, match rules beyond class names, auto-numbering, and external code execution. A module that matches an element still resolves its template via the template chain (by class name), unless it returns rendered output directly (external modules with `"action": "rendered"`).


# External modules

Modules with a `run` field execute an external program. The runtime is determined by the file extension:

- `.wasm` -- executed in the Extism WASM runtime (sandboxed, portable)
- Anything else (`.sh`, `.py`, `.rb`, etc.) -- executed as a subprocess

## Protocol

External modules communicate via JSON on stdin/stdout.

**Element modules** (`span`, `element_children`, `element`) receive a JSON object describing the matched element:

```json
{
  "name": "sidenote",
  "kind": "element_children",
  "writer": "html",
  "context": "div",
  "content": "<p>The rendered children...</p>",
  "classes": ["sidenote"],
  "id": "sn-1",
  "attrs": {"ref": "fn1"},
  "number": 3,
  "vars": {"sidenote_style": "margin"}
}
```

And return a JSON result:

```json
{
  "action": "rendered",
  "output": "<aside class=\"sidenote\">...</aside>"
}
```

The `action` field controls what happens next:

| `action` | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"rendered"` | Use `output` as the final rendering. Stop further dispatch. |
| `"pass"` | This module declines. Continue to the next matching module or fallback template. |

**Document modules** (`document`) receive the full document:

```json
{
  "name": "rewrite-links",
  "kind": "document",
  "writer": "html",
  "body": "<!DOCTYPE html>...",
  "vars": {}
}
```

And return the transformed document in the same `action`/`output` structure.

Document modules can also use a plain text protocol: raw document on stdin, transformed document on stdout (no JSON). Declare this in the manifest:

```toml
[[modules]]
name = "rewrite-links"
kind = "document"
run = "scripts/rewrite-links.sh"
protocol = "text"                    # "json" (default) or "text"
```

**Project modules** (`project`) receive all rendered pages at once:

```json
{
  "name": "site_wrap",
  "kind": "project",
  "writer": "html",
  "pages": [
    {
      "source": "index.qmd",
      "output": "index.html",
      "body": "<article>...</article>",
      "title": "Home",
      "url": "/index.html"
    }
  ],
  "config": { "contents": [...] },
  "vars": {}
}
```

And return the transformed pages:

```json
{
  "action": "rendered",
  "pages": [
    { "output": "index.html", "body": "<!DOCTYPE html>..." }
  ]
}
```

Project modules can add pages to the output (e.g., pagination pages) by including new entries in the `pages` array.


# Installation

Extensions live in `{stem}_calepin/extensions/{name}/`:

```
project/
  index_calepin/
    config.toml
    extensions/
      tufte/
        extension.toml
        templates/...
        assets/...
      lightbox/
        extension.toml
        assets/...
```

A future `calepin install` command could fetch extensions from a registry or git URL. For now, copy or clone the directory manually.


# Activation

An extension that defines a target is activated by using it as the target name in document front matter or via CLI (`-t`):

```toml
# document front matter (e.g., index.qmd)
target = "tufte"
```

An extension that only provides modules or assets (no custom target) is activated by listing it:

```toml
[calepin]
extensions = ["lightbox"]
```

When `extensions` is set, those extensions' assets are included and their modules are available (they run when they match elements by class/attr/id, or when listed in the active target's `modules` field).


# Resolution order

## Templates

First match wins:

1. Document sidecar: `{stem}_calepin/templates/{target|writer|common}/`
2. Project overrides: `{stem}_calepin/templates/{target|writer|common}/`
3. Active extension's templates: `{stem}_calepin/extensions/{name}/templates/{writer|common}/`
4. Parent extension's templates (walking up the inheritance chain)
5. Built-in templates (embedded in binary)

At each level, the lookup order within the templates directory is:

1. `{target}/{name}.{ext}` (target-specific, e.g., `tufte/page.html`)
2. `{writer}/{name}.{ext}` (writer-specific, e.g., `html/page.html`)
3. `common/{name}.jinja` (writer-agnostic)

## Assets

Assets compose additively (all levels contribute):

1. Project assets: `{stem}_calepin/assets/` (always included)
2. Active extension's assets (CSS/JS declared in manifest)
3. Parent extension's assets (walking up the inheritance chain)
4. Built-in assets (embedded in binary, fill gaps)

CSS and JS from multiple extensions are concatenated in inheritance order (parent first, child last), so the child's styles override the parent's. Static files from extensions are copied to `assets/` in the output directory. If two extensions provide a file at the same path, the child's file wins.

## Modules

Modules are resolved from:

1. Active extension's `[[modules]]` entries (declared in its `extension.toml`)
2. Parent extension's `[[modules]]` entries (walking up the inheritance chain)
3. Built-in modules (embedded in binary)

Module templates are resolved via the standard template resolution chain (see above). A module's matched class name determines the template lookup.

A module must be listed in the active target's `modules` field to run as a document/element transform. Modules that match by class/attr/id (span transforms, element children transforms) run whenever a matching element is encountered, regardless of the `modules` list.


# Built-in targets

The built-in targets form this inheritance tree:

```
html                    writer = "html"
  slides                inherits = "html"
  website               inherits = "html"
  book                  inherits = "html"
latex                   writer = "latex"
typst                   writer = "typst"
markdown                writer = "markdown"
```

The base targets (`html`, `latex`, `typst`, `markdown`) each define a writer and a default set of modules, templates, and settings. The composed targets (`slides`, `website`, `book`) inherit from a base and add behavior through modules.

There is no separate "notebook" vs. "collection" type. The pipeline is always the same:

```
1. resolve_pages(config)           # 1 page if no [[contents]], N otherwise
2. for each page (parallel):
     parse -> evaluate -> render -> assemble_page -> transform_document
3. transform_project(all_pages)    # project modules run here (if any)
4. write all pages
5. copy assets
6. run post commands
```

For single documents, step 1 yields one page and step 3 is a no-op. For websites and books, step 1 discovers pages from `[[contents]]` and step 3 runs project modules that handle navigation, cross-references, or orchestrator assembly.

Internally, all built-in targets are structured as extensions:

```
html/
  extension.toml        # writer = "html"
  templates/
    html/
      page.html
      code_source.html
      figure.html
      ...

latex/
  extension.toml        # writer = "latex"
  templates/
    latex/
      page.tex
      ...

slides/
  extension.toml        # inherits = "html"
  templates/
    slides/
      page.html         # overrides html/page.html

website/
  extension.toml        # inherits = "html"
  templates/
    website/
      base.html
      navbar.html
      sidebar.html
  assets/
    calepin.css
    css/...
    fontawesome/...

book/
  extension.toml        # inherits = "html"
  templates/
    book/
      orchestrator.typ
```

What makes `website` and `book` different from `html` is not a type flag -- it is the project modules they declare:

- **`website`** declares `site_wrap` (wraps each page in the site template with navbar, sidebar, prev/next, breadcrumbs) and `crossref_global` (resolves cross-references across pages with chapter-qualified numbering).
- **`book`** declares `orchestrator` (assembles chapter fragments into a master file for PDF compilation).
- **`slides`** has no project modules. It just overrides `page.html` and adds `split_slides` to the per-page document modules.
- A user extension inherits from any of these and follows the same rules.


# Scaffolding

Scaffold a new extension directory:

```
calepin init extension sidenotes --inherits html
```

This creates:

```
sidenotes/
  extension.toml
  templates/
    html/
      .gitkeep
  assets/
    .gitkeep
```

With a starter `extension.toml`:

```toml
name = "sidenotes"
description = ""
version = "0.1.0"
inherits = "html"

[target]
# modules = ["highlight", "append_footnotes", "embed_images"]

[assets]
# css = []
# js = []

# Declare [[modules]] only if you need structural transforms,
# match rules beyond class names, auto-numbering, or external code.
# For simple div styles, just add a template.
```

Then:

1. Add templates to `templates/html/` to override page templates or add new div styles (e.g., `sidenote.html`).
2. Declare modules in `extension.toml` under `[[modules]]`.
3. Add CSS/JS to `assets/` and declare them in `extension.toml`.
4. Copy the directory into a project's `{stem}_calepin/extensions/` to install it.


# Examples

## Visual theme (CSS-only)

```
dark-academic/
  extension.toml
  assets/
    dark-academic.css
```

```toml
name = "dark-academic"
description = "Dark color scheme with serif typography"
version = "1.0.0"
inherits = "html"

[assets]
css = ["dark-academic.css"]
```

No templates, no modules, no target overrides. Activated with `target = "dark-academic"` in document front matter, `-t dark-academic` on the CLI, or `calepin.extensions = ["dark-academic"]`.

## Presentation target

```
slidev/
  extension.toml
  templates/
    html/
      page.html
  assets/
    slidev.css
    slidev.js
  scripts/
    slidev.wasm
```

```toml
name = "slidev"
description = "Slidev-compatible HTML presentations"
version = "0.2.0"
inherits = "slides"

[target]
modules = ["highlight", "append_footnotes", "split_slides"]
standalone = false

[vars]
transition = "slide"    # {{ vars.slidev.transition }}

[assets]
css = ["slidev.css"]
js = ["slidev.js"]
```

Inherits from `slides` (which inherits from `html`). Overrides `page.html` for its own slide shell. The inheritance chain is `slidev -> slides -> html`.

## Academic journal target

```
jss/
  extension.toml
  templates/
    latex/
      page.tex
      code_source.tex
  assets/
    jss.cls
    jss.bst
```

```toml
name = "jss"
description = "Journal of Statistical Software article format"
version = "1.0.0"
inherits = "latex"

[target]
modules = ["highlight", "convert_svg_pdf"]
fig_extension = "pdf"

[vars]
documentclass = "jss"   # {{ vars.jss.documentclass }}

[assets]
static = ["jss.cls", "jss.bst"]
```

Overrides the LaTeX page template and code rendering. Copies `.cls` and `.bst` files alongside the output.

## PDF via post-processing

```
pdf/
  extension.toml
```

```toml
name = "pdf"
description = "PDF output via Typst compilation"
version = "1.0.0"
inherits = "typst"

[target]
extension = "pdf"
post = ["typst compile {input}"]
```

No templates, no assets, no modules. Just inherits everything from `typst` and adds a post-processing step. A user who prefers LaTeX-based PDF would write `inherits = "latex"` and `post = ["tectonic {input}"]` instead.

## Structural module

```
lightbox/
  extension.toml
  templates/
    html/
      lightbox.html
  assets/
    lightbox.css
    lightbox.js
```

```toml
name = "lightbox"
description = "Click-to-zoom image lightbox for HTML figures"
version = "1.0.0"
inherits = "html"

[assets]
css = ["lightbox.css"]
js = ["lightbox.js"]

[[modules]]
name = "lightbox"
description = "Wrap figure images in click-to-zoom lightbox links"
kind = "element_children"
contexts = ["div"]

[modules.match]
classes = ["lightbox"]
writers = ["html"]
```

The template at `templates/html/lightbox.html` is resolved by class name through the standard template chain. Activated with `calepin.extensions = ["lightbox"]`.


# Design constraints

- **Single inheritance only.** One chain: child -> parent -> grandparent -> built-in base target. No diamond inheritance, no multiple parents.
- **Full module list replacement.** If an extension specifies `modules` in `[target]`, it replaces the parent's list entirely. No `modules_add`, no ordering ambiguity.
- **Explicit everything.** The manifest is the complete index. CSS, JS, static files, and modules must be declared in `extension.toml`. No implicit directory scanning.
- **No config fragments.** An extension provides a target definition, templates, modules, and assets. Document-level config (title, author, bibliography, execute options) stays in the document or project config.
- **Additive template chain.** Each level in the chain can override templates from the level below. The user always has final say (project `{stem}_calepin/templates/` overrides everything).
- **Modules are for behavior, templates are for presentation.** Adding a template to `templates/` is enough for custom div/span styles. A `[[modules]]` declaration is only needed for structural transforms, advanced matching, auto-numbering, or external code.
- **One pipeline.** There is no separate "collection" or "notebook" mode. The same pipeline handles 1 page or 1000 pages. Multi-document features (navigation, cross-references, orchestrator assembly) are `project` modules declared by the extension, not a different code path.


# Template resolution in practice

Templates use layered resolution. You only create the files you want to change. Everything else falls through to the extension, its parent, and ultimately the built-in defaults.

## Example: customizing figures

Suppose you have a website and want to change how figures render. You do not need to copy or even know about the other ~50 templates. Create one file:

```
my-site/
  index_calepin/
    config.toml
    templates/
      html/
        figure.html       # just this file
  index.qmd
  about.qmd
```

Your `figure.html`:

```html
<figure id="{{ id }}" class="{{ classes }}">
  <img src="{{ src }}" alt="{{ alt }}" style="border-radius: 8px" />
  {% if caption %}<figcaption>{{ caption }}</figcaption>{% endif %}
</figure>
```

All other templates (`page.html`, `code_source.html`, `callout.html`, etc.) come from the built-in `website` extension. Your override applies only to figures.

The same principle applies to extensions. A "tufte" extension that changes `page.html` and `figure.html` ships only those two files. The remaining templates come from its parent (`html`).

## Debugging resolution

To see where each template is resolved from, run:

```
calepin templates list html
```

Or for a specific target:

```
calepin templates list website
```

This prints the full resolution chain, color-coded by source:

```
page.html          index_calepin/templates/website/page.html    (green = user override)
figure.html        index_calepin/templates/html/figure.html     (green = user override)
code_source.html   built-in: html                         (cyan = built-in)
callout.html       built-in: html                         (cyan = built-in)
...
```

## Template resolution

`calepin init my-site -t website` creates a project config, starter pages, and all templates in `index_calepin/templates/`. When a sidecar exists with templates, only the sidecar templates are used. When no sidecar exists, only the built-in templates are used. There is no mixing between the two sources.
